item.title: Hear This Strange Cough? Here's What May Help
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Kennel cough is a highly contagious respiratory infection that commonly causes a dry, hacking, or honking cough, along with symptoms like sneezing, nasal discharge, and mild lethargy
  • The condition is usually caused by bacteria, viruses, or a combination of infectious organisms that spread when dogs are in close contact with one another
  • Dogs that spend time in kennels, daycares, shelters, dog parks, grooming salons, and other crowded settings face a higher risk of exposure
  • Supportive home care such as rest, hydration, steam therapy, proper nutrition, and throat-soothing remedies may help ease discomfort while your dog's body recovers
  • Puppies, senior dogs, and dogs with worsening symptoms should be evaluated by a veterinarian

You hear it from across the room: a loud, dry cough that sounds like your dog has something stuck in their throat. It's hard not to worry, especially when it seems to come out of nowhere. If that sound is new to you, kennel cough may be the reason. Here's what pet parents should know.

What Is Kennel Cough?

According to My Pet Nutritionist, kennel cough, more accurately known as canine infectious respiratory disease (CIRD), is a highly contagious disease complex caused by a variety of infectious agents.1

These pathogens cause inflammation in the respiratory tract, leading to the condition's hallmark symptom: a persistent dry, hacking, or honking cough.

Dogs with kennel cough may also experience gagging or retching after coughing, sneezing, a runny nose, mild lethargy, reduced appetite, and, in more severe cases, a mild fever.2 The good news is that most healthy dogs recover without major complications. Many cases resolve on their own within 10 to 14 days,3 provided more serious infections or complications do not develop.

Where Does Kennel Cough Come From?

Kennel cough is a little different from many illnesses because it often isn't caused by a single organism. According to an article from the Natchez Trace Veterinary Services website, one of the most common bacterial culprits is Bordetella bronchiseptica. This bacterium attaches to the lining of the respiratory tract, irritating the airways and triggering coughing. Because it spreads efficiently through respiratory droplets and close contact, it can move quickly through groups of dogs.4

Viruses are often involved as well. Common contributors include canine parainfluenza virus and canine adenovirus type 2, while canine distemper virus and canine herpesvirus-1 have also been linked to canine infectious respiratory disease.

When multiple infectious agents work together, symptoms may become more noticeable and recovery can take longer. The infection can spread through:

  • Direct contact with infected dogs
  • Airborne droplets released through coughing or sneezing
  • Shared water bowls and food dishes
  • Contaminated toys, bedding, or surfaces

Which Dogs Face the Greatest Risk?

Any dog can develop kennel cough, but some circumstances make exposure more likely than others. Dogs that spend time in crowded environments, including boarding kennels, animal shelters, dog parks, grooming facilities, doggy daycares, and training classes, face a greater risk because infectious organisms spread more easily when dogs are housed or socialized together. Stress may also increase susceptibility to infection, as physical and emotional stress can affect immune function.5

Age and overall health matter too. Puppies and senior dogs often have a harder time fighting off respiratory infections because their immune systems may not be as robust as those of healthy adult dogs. Dogs with pre-existing medical conditions can also be more vulnerable and may face a greater risk of developing more severe symptoms.

While exposure isn't always avoidable, a healthy immune system remains one of a dog's first lines of defense against infectious disease. Supporting your dog's overall health may help reduce their susceptibility to infection and better prepare their body to respond when exposure occurs.

Natural Ways to Support Your Dog During Recovery

If your veterinarian determines that your dog's case is mild, supportive care at home may help keep them comfortable while their body works through the infection.6,7,8

  1. Honey — Honey is one of the most commonly used home remedies for kennel cough. It contains antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory compounds that may help soothe irritated throat tissues and provide temporary relief from coughing.

    Manuka honey has attracted attention for its antibacterial properties and its ability to inhibit certain pathogens. While it isn't a cure for kennel cough, many pet parents find it helpful for easing throat irritation.
  2. Steam therapy — Moist air may help reduce irritation in the respiratory tract and make breathing more comfortable. Running a humidifier near your dog's resting area or sitting with them in a steam-filled bathroom after a hot shower are simple ways to increase humidity and help soothe inflamed airways during recovery.
  3. Proper nutrition for a stronger immune system — A healthy immune system is one of your dog's first lines of defense against kennel cough and other respiratory infections. Nutrition plays an important role in maintaining healthy immune function, and several vitamins and minerals help support the body's response to illness. Key nutrients include:Chicken bone broth can also be a useful addition because it provides hydration along with gelatin, chondroitin, and other nutrients that support overall health and immune function.
      • Vitamin C — Helps support immune defense by encouraging the production of infection-fighting white blood cells. Sources include blueberries, seaweed, peppers, sweet potatoes, and pumpkin.
      • Vitamin A — Helps maintain the health of the respiratory tract and other protective barriers throughout the body. Sources include liver, fish oil, and egg yolks.
      • Vitamin B6 — Supports normal immune function and plays a role in the body's response to infection. Sources include beef, chicken, turkey, sardines, salmon, and organ meats.
      • Zinc — Helps support immune cell activity while maintaining the integrity of the skin and mucous membranes. Sources include seafood, meat, and fish.
      • Vitamin D — Supports immune function and helps the body respond to infectious organisms. Sources include liver, fish, egg yolks, and mushrooms.
  4. Gentle herbal support — Some integrative practitioners use herbs as part of a supportive care plan for dogs with kennel cough. Common options include:As with any supplement or herbal product, it's best to speak with your veterinarian before introducing new remedies.
    • Licorice root tea — Is known for its soothing and anti-inflammatory properties and may help ease throat irritation.
    • Thyme — Has traditionally been used for its antibacterial and antiviral properties.
    • Chamomile — May help soothe irritated mucous membranes and respiratory tissues.
    • Slippery elm gruel — It's known to form a soothing coating over irritated tissues and is sometimes used to help manage persistent coughing.
  5. Essential oils — Some holistic veterinarians use essential oils as part of a supportive care plan for dogs with kennel cough. When properly diluted, oils such as frankincense and lavender may be applied topically, while certain oil blends are sometimes diffused in the home to help create a more comfortable environment during recovery.

    Because essential oils can be irritating or unsafe if used incorrectly, always consult your veterinarian and follow appropriate dilution guidelines before using them with your dog.
  6. Let your dog rest — One of the simplest and most effective tools for recovery is rest. Healing takes energy, and dogs recovering from illness often benefit from extra downtime. Limiting strenuous exercise, rough play, and overly exciting activities can help your dog recover more comfortably.

Try These Simple Home-Care Tips Too

Rover lists a few practical adjustments around the house can help reduce irritation and keep your dog more comfortable while they recover. Keep these tips in mind:9

  • Encourage plenty of fluids — Staying hydrated is especially important when your dog is dealing with a respiratory infection. Water helps soothe the throat and keeps airway secretions from becoming overly thick. If your dog seems reluctant to drink, low-sodium chicken broth or dog-safe bone broth may help encourage fluid intake.
  • Offer soft or wet food — A sore throat can make crunchy food less appealing. Soft or wet food may be easier and more comfortable for your dog to eat while they're coughing. The added moisture can also help support hydration.
  • Reach for a harness — If your dog needs walks during recovery, use a harness. Collars can place pressure on an already irritated throat, potentially triggering more coughing. A properly fitted harness distributes pressure across the chest instead of the trachea.
  • Keep activity low-key — Recovery takes energy. Providing a calm, comfortable place to rest and temporarily cutting back on strenuous exercise, rough play, and overly exciting activities can help support the healing process.
  • Avoid these irritants — Smoke and strong odors can further irritate inflamed airways and worsen coughing. Try to keep your dog away from:
    • Cigarette smoke
    • Wildfire smoke
    • Fire pits
    • Harsh cleaning products
    • Aerosol sprays
    • Strong fragrances

When Is It Time to Call the Vet?

Most cases of kennel cough improve with supportive care at home, but some dogs need veterinary attention. Contact your veterinarian if your dog develops a fever, loses interest in food, becomes unusually lethargic, shows signs of labored breathing, or if the cough hasn't started to improve after about a week.10

Because kennel cough is highly contagious, keep your dog away from other dogs for about two weeks after symptoms appear, even if they seem to be feeling better sooner. Depending on your dog's condition, your veterinarian may recommend treatments such as a cough suppressant, an anti-inflammatory medication, or antibiotics if a bacterial infection is suspected.

While kennel cough often sounds worse than it is, trust your instincts. If something doesn't seem right, a call to your veterinarian can provide peace of mind and help your dog get the care they need.

Sources and References

  • 1, 7 My Pet Nutritionist, July 11, 2022.
  • 2, 4, 5, 6 Natchez Trace Veterinary Services, PLC, July 29, 2024.
  • 3 PetMD, October 14, 2025.
  • 8, 9, 10 Rover, February 3, 2025.

item.title: What Your Dog Reveals About Your Stress, Health, and Behavior
item.description:
STORY-AT-A-GLANCE

  • When you and your dog look at each other, levels of the hormone oxytocin — sometimes described as the love hormone — increase in both you and your dog
  • Dogs can discriminate between emotional expressions on human faces and body postures
  • Dogs distinguish between the verbal and emotional components of speech and process emotional cues and meanings of words in different hemispheres of the brain, similar to humans
  • Dogs and their owners have synchronized long-term stress levels, and dogs are more likely to be overweight if their owners are, too
  • People who own dogs have a lower risk of heart disease and a lower risk of premature death than non-dog owners, with the benefit being particularly pronounced among singles

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published September 19, 2019.

Dogs have an uncanny way of weaving themselves into our hearts, and it’s not just because they’re cuddly or cute. When you look in a dog’s eyes, you may feel a sense of understanding and kinship that’s hard to describe, and the feeling is prevalent among dog owners. The 2018 Pets and People Survey, which involved more than 1,000 dog owners, revealed 95% view their dog as part of the family, 62% say their dog helps them de-stress after work and 55% believe their dog gives them emotional comfort if they’ve received bad news.1

In fact, dogs engage in “human-like modes of communication,” such as mutual gazing. When you and your dog look at each other, levels of the hormone oxytocin — sometimes described as the love hormone — increase in both you and your dog.2 The warm feelings from oxytocin serve to reinforce the attachment you feel, and this is only the beginning of the intense connections felt between dogs and people.

Dogs Recognize Human Emotions

If it seems like your dog knows what you’re thinking, it’s because he’s likely in tune with your emotional state. Dogs can discriminate between emotional expressions on human faces and body postures. For instance, research published in Biology Letters found dogs recognize both dog and human emotions.3

In one study, dogs were shown human faces with happy and playful expressions or angry and aggressive expressions, paired with a positive, negative or neutral vocalization.

The dogs looked significantly longer at the faces that matched up to the appropriate vocalization, which is an ability previously thought to be distinct to humans. According to the study, the fact that dogs are able to gain emotional information from both visual and auditory cues, and use them to perceive emotions, is significant:4

“It is likely that dogs possess at least the mental prototypes for emotional categorization (positive versus negative affect) and can recognize the emotional content of these expressions. Moreover, dogs performed in this way without any training or familiarization with the models, suggesting that these emotional signals are intrinsically important.”

Dogs May Process Speech Like You Do

Dogs often watch your every move, paying attention to the emotional cues in your voice and those indicated via your body language. They can distinguish between the verbal and emotional components of speech and process emotional cues and meanings of words in different hemispheres of the brain, similar to humans.5

At the same time, while your dog is intently listening to you, owners also understand their dog’s barks. For instance, in a study involving a Hungarian dog breed called Mudi,6 researchers recorded the dogs barking in six distinct situations, including:7

• A stranger at the door

• A “bad guy” triggering aggression

• An owner picking up the dog’s leash for a walk

• The dog left alone while tied to a tree

• Playing tug-of-war with his owner

• The owner holding a toy near the dog

The recordings were then played for 36 people, who were able to categorize the barks according to the dogs’ likely emotions at the time (playful, fearful or aggressive).

Study author Péter Pongrácz, Ph.D., of Eötvös Loránd University in Hungary, told the American Psychological Association dogs are “a very special, man-created animal," adding, "It was shaped during many tens of thousands of years of domestication to live with people, so it's not surprising that this type of communication should exist."8 Karen B. London, Ph.D., a certified applied animal behaviorist and certified professional dog trainer, agreed, telling Bark:9

“Just as we understand dog vocalizations, they are able to make sense of ours, and are responsive to our tone of voice as well as our words. In both human and canine brains, the same area of the temporal lobe responds to human speech; crying and laughing, as well as canine whimpers and intense barking, cause activity near the primary auditory cortex of both species.
So, it’s a simple biological fact that physiologically, visually, acoustically and cerebrally, humans and dogs just get each other. The closeness we feel to dogs is a natural outcome of that biological connection.”

Dogs and Owners Have Synchronized Stress Levels

Dogs and their owners are so connected that even their stress levels are similar. While it’s previously been demonstrated that acute stress episodes are “contagious” among humans as well as among other species, researchers looked into the long-term stress levels of 58 dog-owner pairs.

Significant correlations were found in long-term stress levels among the humans and their dogs. Further, certain human personality traits — namely neuroticism, conscientiousness and openness, significantly affected dogs’ stress levels, as measured by hair cortisol concentrations. According to the study, “Hence, we suggest that dogs, to a great extent, mirror the stress level of their owners.”10

Veterinarians also commonly observe that pet parents often display many of the same health conditions as their pets, such as obesity or heart problems, which may be linked to similarities in processed food diets or lack of activity.11

“The trend of processed foods and everything that occurs with industrialization is making us both sick,” Dr. Joseph Bartges, professor of veterinary medicine at the University of Georgia, told the Seattle Times, adding, “As veterinarians, we often see pets who have the same health issues as their human companions or who are sentinels for a human health problem.”12

Dogs, for instance, are more likely to be overweight if their owners are, too.13 The good news is that having a dog in your life is beneficial to your health, physically and mentally. People who own dogs have a lower risk of heart disease and a lower risk of premature death than non-dog owners, with the benefit being particularly pronounced among singles.14

What’s more, for those struggling with mental illness, pets provide a distraction from distressing symptoms, facilitate daily routine and exercise, and offer acceptance and unconditional love. The data is so convincing that researchers have concluded:15

“Pets should be considered a main rather than a marginal source of support in the management of long-term mental health problems.”

In case there were any doubt, the close ties between humans and their dogs continue to be revealed, but if you’re a dog owner, you don’t need to be told that — just go spend time with your dog, and you’ll readily feel it!

Sources and References

  • 1 Purina July 11, 2018
  • 2 Science. 2015 Apr 17;348(6232):333-6
  • 3, 4 Biol Lett. 2016 Jan;12(1):20150883
  • 5 Current Biology December 15, 2014
  • 6 J Comp Psychol. 2005 May;119(2):136-44
  • 7, 8 American Psychological Association 2005
  • 9 Bark July 2019
  • 10 Sci Rep. 2019; 9: 7391
  • 11, 12 Seattle Times August 6, 2019
  • 13 Public Health Nutrition January 2010, Volume 13, Issue 1, pp. 102-106
  • 14 Scientific Reports Volume 7, Article number: 15821 (2017)
  • 15 BMC Psychiatry December 9, 2016

item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Probiotics are strains of gut-friendly live microorganisms that your pet can obtain from food sources or supplements

  • There are emerging studies that found soil-based organisms (SBOs) to be beneficial for animals, especially those with gut issues like diarrhea associated with inflammatory bowel syndrome (IBS)

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published October 2, 2018.

A healthy gut microbiome is an essential foundation for your pet’s optimal health. Unfortunately, there are many factors that can disrupt the ratio of good-to-bad bacteria in their gut, including:

  • A biologically inappropriate diet, genetically engineered foods, glyphosate and other food production chemicals
  • Vaccinations, antibiotics, dewormers, flea, tick and heartworm pesticides and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) medications
  • Emotional stress caused by change in routine or environment
  • Consumption of nonfood items or contaminated water
  • Sudden change in diet
  • Gastrointestinal (GI) disease

To ensure that your animal companion has a healthy population of bacteria in their GI system, provide them with a variety of probiotic sources. Probiotics are strains of gut-friendly live microorganisms that your pet can obtain from food sources or supplements. Read on to learn the best sources of probiotics for your animal companion.

Did You Know?

The word “probiotic” is coined from the Latin word “pro” and the Greek word “bios,” which together means “for life.”1 The German scientist Werner Kollath introduced this word in 1953, referring to “active substances that are essential for a healthy development of life.”2

What Are Pet-Friendly Bacteria Strains?

The strains of bacteria that are beneficial to pets are unique to their own species. Some of the strains that have been found to promote healthy gut balance in dogs and cats include:3,4

  • Bifidobacterium lactis
  • Streptococcus thermophilus
  • Lactobacillus acidophilus
  • Saccharomyces boulardii
  • Bifidobacterium bifidum
  • Enterococcus faecium
  • Lactobacillus casei
  • Lactobacillus rhamnosus
  • Lactobacillus plantarum
  • Lactobacillus bulgaricus
  • Bifidobacterium breve
  • Bacillus sporogenes

Giving your pet a diverse source of probiotics, whether nutritional or supplemental, lets them have a rotation of these beneficial bacteria.

Better Digestion and Lower Risk of GI Issues for Your Pets

By reestablishing a balanced ratio of good-to-bad bacteria in your pet’s gut, probiotics may help promote optimal digestive function and reduce your pet’s risk of GI disorders. Several studies have shown that probiotics can be useful for managing the symptoms and decreasing the duration of diarrhea in dogs. It may help lower the incidence of acute and diet-related canine diarrhea as well.5,6,7

Similar results have been observed in feline studies. For instance, a study published in the Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery found that 72% of owners noticed an improvement in their cat’s diarrhea after 21 days of probiotic therapy.8

Another study that evaluated the effects of the probiotic Enterococcus faecium found that cats given probiotics have lower incidence rates of feline diarrhea compared to cats in the placebo group, which suggests that probiotics may be beneficial for relieving feline inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs).9

A Healthy Gut Means a Strong Immunity and Mental Health

Your pet’s digestive tract is the largest immune organ in their body, and it contains even more intestinal bacteria than yours does.10 By optimizing their gut microbiome, you’re also helping improve their immune function. According to an article published in Current Opinion in Gastroenterology:11

“Probiotics play a role in defining and maintaining the delicate balance between necessary and excessive defense mechanisms including innate and adaptive immune responses … Regulation of gene expression and signaling pathways in the host cells are two major mechanisms underlying probiotic action leading to immunomodulation.”

Your pet’s GI tract is also connected to their brain. In fact, it contributes to the production of serotonin,12 an essential hormone for your pet’s cognitive and behavioral functions.13 According to a study in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, probiotics help improve cognitive function in both animals and humans, and may be useful in ameliorating cognitive disorders.14

Probiotics Have Allergy-Fighting Properties

Probiotics are known to have anti-inflammatory properties that may help alleviate the symptoms of skin allergies in animals.15 A study published in the journal Veterinary Immunology and Immunopathology suggests that exposure to probiotics early in life may help lower a dog’s risk of atopic dermatitis.16

A Frontiers in Microbiology study conducted on cats also found that oral probiotics may help modulate respiratory microbiota, making it a potential tool for targeting the dysbiosis caused by inflammatory airway diseases like feline asthma.17

Probiotic Fun Fact

The concept of good bacteria was first introduced in 1907 by Russian scientist and Nobel Prize winner Elie Metchnikoff.18 He determined the health benefits of the microbes responsible for the fermentation process and associated enhanced longevity with the regular consumption of fermented dairy such as yogurt.19

Add These Natural Sources of Probiotics to Your Pet’s Diet

Ideally, pets should get the majority of their nutritional needs, including probiotics, from fresh, whole foods. Below are probiotic-filled foods that you can add to your pet’s nutritionally balanced, species-appropriate diet. You can also give these as a treat, but make sure to limit these “extras” to 10% of your pet’s daily caloric intake.

  • Grass fed plain yogurt — Yogurt has long been known as an excellent source of beneficial probiotics. Aside from live cultures, it can also provide your pet with calcium, B vitamins and cancer-fighting conjugated linoleic acid (CLA).20,21 If you’re planning to buy yogurt, choose a brand that’s organic, unflavored and made from pastured milk. Better yet, make your own yogurt at home using a starter culture and raw grass fed milk.
  • Kefir — Made from the mixture of raw milk or coconut water and live cultures of beneficial yeasts and bacteria called “kefir grains,” this fermented beverage may contain up to 61 strains of probiotics.22 Adding this to your pet’s diet is one of the best and least expensive ways to increase their probiotic intake.

    You can make kefir at home by simply adding a half packet of kefir starter granules to a quart of raw grass fed milk. Allow the mixture to ferment at room temperature overnight, and then strain the kefir into a clean container. Add 1 to 3 teaspoons of kefir to your pet’s food once or twice a day for optimal GI health. You can also make or buy coconut kefir, if your pet is allergic to dairy products.
  • Fermented vegetables — Traditionally cultured vegetables are inherently rich in vitamins and phytochemicals, which become more bioavailable because of the fermentation process. They also provide antioxidant properties that help boost your pet’s immunity and protect them against diseases.23,24

    You can find fermented vegetables at some grocery stores and specialty markets (make sure they’re onion-free and unpasteurized), but it’s cheaper and easier to make your own at home. When adding fermented vegetables to your pet’s diet, start with small amounts to gradually increase their tolerance, especially if it’s their first time having this food. Pets can eat up to 3 teaspoons of fermented vegetables per 20 pounds of body weight.

Should You Buy Commercial Pet Food with Probiotics?

There are many types of probiotics, and some live cultures can be sensitive to heat, moisture and processing techniques, so if these microorganisms are added to pet foods pre-production, then the manufacturing process will kill off most of them and will render them useless.

“Research shows that out of 19 commercial pet foods tested for their probiotic claim, not one product contained any of the listed microorganisms on its label.”25

It is much more beneficial for your pet to consume probiotic-rich foods rather than a highly refined commercial pet food that has tiny amounts of probiotics along with a laundry list of other harmful ingredients.

What Was the First Probiotic Discovered?

The first probiotic strain discovered was Bacillus bulgaricus (now known as Lactobacillus bulgaricus), a lactic acid bacteria identified by Stamen Grigorov, a Bulgarian medical student, in 1905.

How to Find the Best Pet Probiotic Supplement

If your pet doesn’t like the taste of foods with natural probiotics, then you may consider giving them a probiotic supplement, which come in powder, paste, pill and liquid forms that you can easily mix in your pet’s meals or hide in soft treats. When choosing a high-quality pet probiotic, look for the following characteristics:

  • Contains the correct strains of bacteria beneficial for pets, not people
  • Easy to administer
  • Has the ability to survive the acidic environment of your pet's stomach
  • Has enough live organisms to colonize the intestines
  • Remains stable under normal storage conditions

Providing a variety of probiotics strains by using different foods and supplements is a wise idea, as maintaining a wide variety of healthy microbes is best achieved by nutritional and supplement diversity.

Be Careful Not to Confuse Probiotics with Prebiotics

Although they sound similar, probiotics and prebiotics are not the same and serve very different purposes. Prebiotic fibers found in a variety of whole foods serve as healthy food sources for gut bacteria. Prebiotics also come in supplement form, including fructooligosaccharides (FOS), inulin and oligofructose.

Many commercial pet food manufacturers market products containing supplemental prebiotics and probiotics. Some brands also claim that prebiotics help nourish gut-friendly bacteria, but this isn’t always the case.

Prebiotic supplements can feed bacterial blooms in the gut and be harmful for pets with small intestinal bacteria overgrowth (SIBO). Prebiotic supplements may exacerbate GI issues in pets, so it’s always safest to feed healthy sources of prebiotic foods, including Jerusalem artichokes, asparagus, and culinary and medicinal mushrooms, instead of giving prebiotic supplements to pets with GI issues.

If you already feed your pet a wide variety of unsprayed or organic fresh fruits and vegetables, offer pro and prebiotic foods and give your pet ample daily access to healthy soil outdoors, you may not need to give prebiotic or probiotic supplements at all.

Another Good Source of Beneficial Bacteria — Healthy Soil

There are emerging studies that found soil-based organisms (SBOs) to be beneficial for animals, especially those with gut issues like diarrhea associated with inflammatory bowel syndrome (IBS).26,27 According to an animal study analysis published in Microorganisms:28

“[S]oil biodiversity is interrelated with the gut microbiome. In particular, the gut microbial diversity in mice was increased by exposure to soil microbes … Results from animal studies suggest that contact with soil and its microbiome is beneficial for healthy gut microbiota.”

The best and most affordable way to give your pet beneficial soil-based bacteria is to maximize their outdoor time. Walk your pet outside regularly and give them access to unsprayed, healthy soil to optimize their gut microbiome.

item.title: Which Is Smarter, Your Cat or Your Dog? Here's What the Study Says
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • A study suggests that cats, like dogs, have episodic memory and may be just as intelligent as their canine counterparts
  • Episodic memory is related to introspection, and according to the lead study author, it could be that cats “may enjoy actively recalling memories of their experience like humans”
  • It’s not easy to compare intelligence between species, but some experts use the Encephalization Quotient (EQ) to compare intelligence and brain weight in relation to an animal’s body size
  • Social animals (dogs) are thought to have higher EQs than solitary animals (kitties), which is why many experts believe dogs are smarter
  • Cats are also more difficult to study than dogs, but researchers have shown they can be trained to distinguish between different quantities of objects and follow pointing gestures, just as dogs do

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 20, 2018.

A Japanese study suggests that since cats are as good as dogs at certain memory tests, they may be just as intelligent as their canine counterparts. The study involved 49 domestic cats and shows they can recall memories of pleasant experiences, such as eating a favorite food.1

A unique memory of a specific event is known as episodic memory, and along with humans, dogs are also capable of having these types of memories, which are linked with an individual's experience of a specific event, and are unique to that individual. According to Bob Yirka, writing for Phys.org:

"Prior research has shown that human beings have what is known as episodic memory, which is the ability to connect autobiographical information with contextual details — an example would be recalling the details of a birthday party, rather than just the fact that it occurred. Part of this memory allows for recalling what happened and when, and that was something the researchers wanted to know if cats have as well — other studies have shown dogs have it."2

Episodic memory differs from semantic memory, which is formed from facts and rules that animals learn in order to survive. According to lead researcher Saho Takagi of Kyoto University, in an interview with BBC News:

"Episodic memory is viewed as being related to introspective function of the mind; our study may imply a type of consciousness in cats. An interesting speculation is that they may enjoy actively recalling memories of their experience like humans."3

Past research suggests primates, pigeons and rats may also form episodic memories.4

Study Suggests Cats and Dogs May Be Equally Intelligent

The researchers fed the cats using multiple bowls of food over time. They learned which types of food the cats preferred and served it to them in a specific bowl, which caused the kitties to form memories of what was served and when. Later, they switched up the bowls to observe whether a given cat remembered such details.

Other experiments the researchers performed showed the kitties were able to remember if they had previously searched a given bowl when looking for a particular type of food and the circumstances under which it occurred. The research team believes cats may remember for much longer periods than their experiments measured, and they also say cats are on a par with dogs on a variety of mental tests, including responding to human gestures, facial expressions and emotions.

"Understanding cats more deeply helps to establish better cat-human relationships," Takagi said. "Cats may be as intelligent as dogs, as opposed to the common view of people that dogs are much smarter."

This research could open the door to additional studies to determine how long cats' memories are, and what other kinds of episodes in their lives they remember. This is very exciting, because cats don't get nearly the research attention or funding that dogs do.

How Accurate Is the Comparison Between Dog and Cat Intelligence?

Dog and cat people have been asking this question for decades, but the question of who's smarter, dogs or cats, is actually a tricky topic to investigate because even the question is problematic. item.title: Could Your Furry Friend Know Exactly What It Needs?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Some animals in the wild seek out and interact with plants in ways that may support their health. Offering indoor cats a selection of dried herbs gives them an opportunity to exercise similar self-selection
  • Cats can interact with herbs through both scent and ingestion, choosing whether to sniff, rub against, roll in, or nibble each plant. Walking away is also part of self-selection and simply means they are not interested in that herb at that time
  • Six dried herbs commonly offered to cats are valerian root, chamomile, catnip, organic rose buds, lemon balm, and hops (used with caution)
  • A cat herb “garden” requires no planting: simply arrange small, separate piles of dried herbs on a clean towel or blanket in a quiet, comfortable area and allow your cat to investigate freely
  • Use plain, correctly identified dried herbs from a trusted source, avoid concentrated preparations such as essential oils, and consult your veterinarian if your cat has an existing health condition

Cats have a reputation for knowing exactly what they want, whether it is their food, their toys, or even their favorite person. That selectiveness may extend to plants as well. In nature, some animals seek out plants and other substances in ways that may support their health.

For instance, research has found that cats rubbing against certain plants transfer compounds onto their coats that help repel mosquitoes.1 This type of voluntary interaction with natural substances may be linked to self-selection, a concept explored within zoopharmacognosy, which studies how animals use naturally occurring substances.2

For indoor cats, this idea can have an interesting application. Much of your cat’s environment is chosen for them, from what they eat and where they sleep to when they receive supplements. Offering a selection of safe herbs gives them a chance to explore different scents and plants — a simple form of enrichment that is easier to set up than you might think.

How to Create an Herb ‘Garden’ for Your Cat

Despite the name, a cat herb garden does not require soil, pots, or any actual gardening. It can be as simple as placing several herbs on a clean towel or blanket. The “garden” simply refers to a small assortment of herbs arranged separately for your cat to explore, much like having several plants available in one space.

To set one up, place several dried herbs on a clean towel or blanket in an area where your cat already feels comfortable, ideally a quiet spot away from heavy foot traffic, loud appliances, or areas where another animal could make your cat feel cornered. Place about a tablespoon of each herb in its own pile, leaving enough space between them for your cat to investigate each one separately.

Keeping the herbs apart also makes it easier to see which ones attract your cat’s attention. Once the herbs are in place, let your cat approach on their own. Avoid placing your cat on the blanket, holding an herb under their nose, or directing them toward a particular pile. Instead, watch which herb they approach first, how they interact with it, and whether they return to it later.

You can leave the garden available in a safe, dry location and refresh the herbs once their aroma begins to fade. If you have more than one cat, consider setting up separate gardens so they can explore without competing for the same space.3,4,5

6 Feline-Friendly Herbs to Explore

Now that you know what a cat herb garden looks like, the next step is choosing what to put in it. Not every cat responds to the same plants, so offering several options gives your cat more room to explore what appeals to them. These six dried herbs provide a range of aromas and plant compounds commonly used for feline self-selection:6,7

  1. Catnip — The response to catnip is genetic, so about 30-40% of cats will not visibly react to it, but for those that do, it remains one of the most reliable enrichment herbs available.8 Catnip contains nepetalactone, the compound responsible for the familiar rolling, rubbing, licking, kicking, and playful behavior seen in responsive cats.9
  2. Valerian root — Valerian contains valerenic acid and other compounds that influence receptors for gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a neurotransmitter involved in calming nervous-system activity. It also contains actinidine, an aromatic compound that can trigger a catnip-like response in some cats. In one feline study, about half of the cats responded to valerian, including some that did not respond to catnip.10
  3. Chamomile — Chamomile contains flavonoids such as apigenin, which has calming activity.11 Cats tend to interact with chamomile quietly compared to valerian or catnip. Rather than rolling or playing, they may rest beside the pile, rest their face near it, or fall asleep on that part of the garden.
  4. Rose buds — Rose has a long history in traditional herbal practice as an herb associated with emotional comfort,12 and it is ideal for sensitive, elderly, or easily overwhelmed cats. Choose plain, organically grown dried rose buds, since florist roses may contain pesticide residues, dyes, preservatives, or other treatments.
  5. Lemon balm — Lemon balm has a light, lemony scent and contains rosmarinic acid and other aromatic compounds. Research on lemon balm extracts has explored effects on GABA-related pathways and anxiety-like behavior in animals.13
  6. Hops — Hops have a stronger, more distinctive aroma and contain compounds including humulone and xanthohumol. Research suggests that some of these compounds may influence GABA-related pathways and sleep regulation.14 Some cats may be attracted to the scent, while others may take one sniff and move on. Please note, hops are dangerously toxic to dogs and can result in malignant hyperthermia which can be fatal. Do not offer hops if there are dogs in the home.

How Your Cat May Respond to Herbs

Cats interact with plant compounds through two main pathways. Aromatic compounds are detected by scent receptors when your cat sniffs a plant, while other compounds can be absorbed through digestion when they nibble or chew it. The same herb can produce different effects depending on how your cat engages with it — catnip, for instance, tends to be stimulating when inhaled and calming when eaten.

Other ways your cat may engage include rolling over the herb, stretching nearby, licking or nibbling a small amount, or settling beside it. Interest can also be much subtler, such as slow blinking, lip licking, swallowing, relaxed breathing, or simply choosing to remain close to the plant. Your cat may also ignore an herb altogether, which can simply mean that particular scent or plant does not appeal to them at that time.

Safety Tips for Offering Herbs to Your Cat

Quality and preparation matter when offering herbs to your cat. Choose organically grown, dried whole herbs from a trusted supplier. Avoid products treated with pesticides, fragrances, preservatives, dyes, or other added ingredients, and make sure you are buying the correct plant and plant part. The herbs need to be dried as some of these herbs contain essential oils in the fresh plant that can be toxic if touched or consumed.

It also helps to look for the herb’s botanical name on the package. Common names are sometimes used for more than one plant, so the scientific name provides another way to confirm exactly what you are offering. Use dried whole herbs only — do not use essential oils, fragrance oils, concentrated extracts, perfumes, and potpourri as substitutes.

If your cat tries to consume a large amount at once, remove the herbs and offer them again later under supervision. Your cat should also be able to leave the area whenever they choose. If they have an unusual physical or behavioral reaction to an herb, remove it and do not offer it again without professional guidance.

Finally, an herb garden is meant for enrichment and self-directed exploration and should never replace veterinary care. A cat’s interest in a particular herb does not explain why they may be feeling unwell. If your cat is ill, taking medication, or has an ongoing health condition, consult your veterinarian before offering any herbs.15,16

Sources and References

  • 2,3,6,15 The Natural Pet Doctor, August 14, 2026
  • 4,7 Naturally Healthy Pets, October 25, 2021
  • 5,16 Meowme, Let Your Cat Choose Her Own Herbs
  • 8 Behav Processes. 2017 Sep:142:110-115
  • 9 The International Cat Association, December 11, 2024
  • 10 BMC Vet Res. 2017 Mar 16;13:70
  • 11 Mol Med Rep. 2010 Nov 1;3(6):895–901
  • 12 Biomolecules. 2021 Jan 19;11(1):127
  • 13 Nutrients. 2024 Oct 18;16(20):3545
  • 14 Journal of Ethnopharmacology, Volume 338, Part 2, 10 February 2025, 119019

item.title: If a Snake Bites Your Pet, Never Do This
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Two incidents of snakebites in dogs provide a timely reminder to all pet parents about the seriousness of this threat
  • Most snakebites in pets happen in their own backyard, and while venomous bites are life-threatening, even a nonvenomous snakebite can be dangerous
  • If a snake bites your pet remember to stay calm, keep the site of the bite below the level of his heart, and immediately drive to the nearest emergency animal hospital
  • To help keep your pet safe from snakebites, it’s important to learn which types of snakes are prevalent in the areas where you live and visit with your animal companion
  • Muscle contractions in dead snakes can leave them capable of biting for several hours after death, so pets should never be allowed near one

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published September 11, 2019.

Two separate snakebite incidents involving dogs and rattlers occurred — one in California and one in Colorado. In the first case, two women and their three dogs were hiking in the desert and exploring mines, when one of the dogs, a 6-year-old Mastiff, was bitten on the foot by a baby rattlesnake.

In a race against time, the women quickly descended the mountain with the three dogs, and somehow located an open veterinary office (it was Sunday) two hours away that had antivenin on hand. When they arrived, the antivenin was still frozen and took another hour to thaw.

The Mastiff received two vials of antivenin (at $500 each) over an extended period of time, and proceeded to make a slow, painful recovery that was complicated by seizures. The final bill was around $3,000.

In the second incident, a dog hiking a trail with her owner sustained three bites from a rattler, at least one of which was on her tongue. Two mountain bikers who happened by helped carry the dog down the mountain to try to control the spread of the venom, and the dog’s owner called around to vet clinics until she found one that stocked the antivenin.

The dog’s bites were the worst the treating veterinarians had ever encountered, and she wound up in ICU, but is expected to make a full recovery.

Believe It or Not, Most Snakebites Happen in the Backyard

The majority of snakebites in companion animals occur in the backyard, where dogs and many cats are allowed to roam around loose. Humans tend to make noise and scare off snakes, whereas pets are more likely to quietly approach and even stalk a snake they encounter on their home turf. If the snake is moving or rattling, it’s an even greater curiosity.

Most pets get bitten on the nose, neck or legs, which are the areas that will naturally be closest to a striking snake. Even nonvenomous snakebites can be quite painful, and bacteria at the bite site can cause a secondary infection. If your pet sustains a snakebite, don’t try to capture or kill the snake to bring it with you. Instead, quickly snap a cell phone picture, or if that’s not possible, take a mental picture so you can provide a physical description of the snake to the vet staff upon your arrival.

item.title: Could One Hormone Explain the Changes in Your Pet?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Cortisol is a hormone from the adrenal glands that does far more than manage stress — it regulates blood sugar, metabolism, inflammation, immune function, and blood pressure
  • Cortisol production follows a natural daily rhythm through the HPA axis — short bursts are healthy and adaptive, but chronic elevation is where the real trouble begins
  • Too much cortisol over time can lead to Cushing’s disease (thirst, hair loss, pot belly, and weakness); too little leads to Addison’s disease (lethargy, vomiting, and potentially fatal collapse)
  • Chronic stress from aversive training, kennels, separation anxiety, or ongoing pain keeps cortisol elevated — linked to anxiety, aggression, immune suppression, and higher cancer risk
  • Positive interactions, consistent routines, positive reinforcement training, enrichment, calming music, and your own calm presence measurably lower cortisol — when you calm down, your pet often calms down too

Your dog has been drinking a lot more water lately. Or your cat is losing weight and seems anxious in ways they never used to be. Or maybe your usually confident dog has become withdrawn, snappy, or hyper-alert to noises that used to slide right past them. Something has shifted, and you cannot quite name it.

Behind many of these subtle changes may sit one busy little hormone: cortisol. It is often called the stress hormone, but that name does not do it justice. Cortisol quietly influences almost every system in your pet’s body, and when its levels drift out of balance, the changes can ripple in surprising directions.

What Is Cortisol?

Cortisol is a steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands — two small glands sitting just above the kidneys. It is part of a class of hormones called glucocorticoids, and it does far more than manage stress. Its major jobs include:1,2

  • Regulating the body’s response to stress and perceived danger
  • Contributing to maintenance of blood sugar and metabolism
  • Managing inflammation throughout the body
  • Supporting and modulating immune responses
  • Influencing blood pressure
  • Helping the body use energy efficiently during activity or challenge

Synthetic versions of cortisol are used as prescription anti-inflammatory medications, which gives you a sense of how powerful this hormone actually is.

How the System Works

Cortisol production is controlled by a three-way conversation between the brain and the adrenal glands, known as the HPA axis (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal).3,4

When a stressor appears — a loud noise, a chaotic environment, or a physical challenge — the hypothalamus in the brain releases a signaling hormone (CRH or corticotropin releasing hormone). That triggers the pituitary gland to release another signal (ACTH or adrenocorticotropic hormone), which travels to the adrenal glands. The adrenals respond by releasing cortisol into the bloodstream.

Cortisol then travels around the body doing its work. When enough of it is circulating, it feeds back to the hypothalamus and pituitary to say, in essence, that is enough for now. The whole system is designed to rise sharply, do its job, and settle back down.

There is also a natural daily rhythm. Cortisol tends to peak in the morning and drop lower in the evening, though environmental factors and individual variability can shift that pattern.

This background rhythm matters. It is why a single blood test can only tell part of the story — sampling time, recent events, and even the stress of the veterinary visit itself can nudge results one way or another. Good clinicians take all of that into account when interpreting what a cortisol number really means.5

Acute vs. Chronic: The Big Distinction

Short bursts of elevated cortisol are healthy and necessary. A sudden loud thunderstorm, a trip to the vet, or a startling encounter with another dog all trigger a rapid cortisol spike — the body mobilizes energy, sharpens focus, and prepares to respond. Once the moment passes, levels return to normal. This is the system doing exactly what it evolved to do.6,7

Problems start when cortisol stays elevated. Chronic stress — a shelter environment, ongoing conflict at home, aversive training, unresolved anxiety, or chronic pain — keeps the HPA axis firing over and over. That prolonged elevation can suppress the immune system, break down muscle, contribute to weight gain, and change behavior in ways that do not reverse easily.

Chronic elevation has even been linked in research to an increased incidence of certain cancers in dogs, particularly in animals with sustained fear, anxiety, or aggression. It is a serious downstream cost of a nervous system that never gets to rest.

When There Is Too Much: Cushing’s Disease

Sometimes cortisol trouble is not about stress at all. It comes from the adrenal system itself producing too much of the hormone, often because of a small tumor on the pituitary or adrenal gland. That condition is called hyperadrenocorticism, better known as Cushing’s disease (primarily for the pituitary form) or Cushing’s syndrome.

It is one of the most common endocrine disorders in middle-aged and older dogs — one U.S. estimate suggests around 100,000 new canine cases each year. It is less common in cats but does occur. Classic signs include:8,9

  • Increased thirst and urination
  • Increased appetite
  • A pot-bellied appearance
  • Thinning skin, hair loss, or a dull coat
  • Muscle weakness
  • Low energy or lethargy
  • Recurring skin or urinary infections

Chronic exposure to elevated cortisol can also worsen diabetes, raise blood pressure, and increase the risk of clot formation. Early detection and treatment matter.

When There Is Too Little: Addison’s Disease

On the other end of the spectrum, the adrenal glands can under-produce cortisol. That is called hypoadrenocorticism, or Addison’s disease, and it is often trickier to diagnose because the symptoms come and go. Watch for:10

  • Lethargy or unusual weakness
  • Vomiting and diarrhea
  • Loss of appetite
  • Shaking or trembling
  • Weight loss
  • In severe cases, collapse or shock (an Addisonian crisis)

An Addisonian crisis is a life-threatening emergency. If your dog collapses suddenly or shows severe weakness, take them to a veterinarian immediately.

Cortisol and Behavior

Because cortisol influences the brain and nervous system so directly, it also shows up in behavior. Chronic elevation is closely linked to anxiety, fearfulness, aggression, and difficulty settling. Dogs with aggressive tendencies have been shown to carry higher baseline cortisol levels. Dogs with separation anxiety show significant cortisol spikes when their humans leave, and juvenile dogs with elevated cortisol tend to struggle more when navigating unfamiliar environments.

On the flip side, dogs in stable, predictable homes — with owners they trust and consistent routines — tend to show more balanced, moderate cortisol patterns. The environment they live in, quite literally, shapes the endocrine world inside them.

There is even an intriguing pattern showing up in research: Shy or cautious animals tend to have higher baseline cortisol, while bolder, more exploratory animals show lower baseline levels but faster spikes when they do encounter stress. Each temperament comes with its own physiology, and there is no single right pattern. What matters is whether the system can return to rest when the challenge is over.11

What Raises and Lowers Cortisol?

Research has identified a fairly consistent list of things that push cortisol up. These include:

  • Aversive training methods (shock collars, leash corrections, and yelling)
  • Kennel or shelter environments, especially with poor enrichment
  • Separation from familiar humans
  • Loud noises or sound sensitivity
  • Inter-dog aggression or unstable social hierarchies
  • Grooming and veterinary procedures without desensitization
  • Chronic pain or illness
  • Unfamiliar environments without a safe base

Just as importantly, research has identified habits and conditions that reliably bring cortisol down, such as:

  • Positive, consistent interactions with familiar humans — petting, play, and calm presence
  • A stable daily routine (predictable meals, walks, and rest times)
  • Positive reinforcement training rather than punishment
  • Group housing with other well-matched dogs when appropriate
  • Classical music in the background of stressful environments
  • Gentle massage after stressful events
  • Enrichment — puzzle feeders, sniff walks, and mental engagement
  • Owner presence during veterinary visits when possible
  • Nutritional support such as L-theanine, alpha-casozepine, or tryptophan, discussed with your vet

Studies have also shown that positive interactions synchronize cortisol between dogs and their humans — when you calm down, your dog calms down. That is a beautiful and underappreciated form of medicine.12

Changes Worth Bringing to Your Veterinarian

If your dog or cat is showing several of the following, especially in combination, it is time for a check-in. None of these signs on their own is necessarily alarming — most can be explained by a dozen unrelated things — but when several show up together, or when they persist over weeks rather than days, cortisol imbalance moves higher on the list of possibilities worth ruling out:

  • Sudden or persistent changes in thirst or urination
  • Noticeable weight gain or loss
  • Appetite changes
  • Coat quality or skin issues, particularly fragile skin that abrades or tears easily
  • Muscle weakness
  • Lethargy or unusual restlessness
  • New anxiety, fearfulness, or aggression
  • Behavior changes that do not have a clear reason

Cortisol-related symptoms can mimic many other conditions, including normal aging. Regular wellness exams are what catch this early. Your veterinarian may recommend blood work, urine testing, or specific stimulation tests to check adrenal function.

How Cortisol Is Measured

Modern veterinary medicine has multiple ways to measure cortisol, from invasive to non-invasive. Blood tests give the most direct snapshot but can be affected by the stress of the blood draw itself. Blood tests give a picture of what is circulating in the bloodstream at that moment in time and are analyzed through different testing protocols, including baseline cortisol, low dose dexamethasone suppression test cortisol, and ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) stimulation testing. Your veterinarian will choose the right test based on what they are trying to learn.

A slightly less invasive test is the urine cortisol-to-creatinine ratio. Often, a first-of-the-morning urine sample caught at home by the pet parents is used to reduce any stress influence. The UCC ratio is useful for evaluating cortisol production over a several hour period of time and is often used to screen for conditions such as Cushing’s disease or chronic stress.

Additional cortisol testing methods are being used in the research sector and have benefit for lowering stress of repeat testing for the research animals. Saliva tests are minimally invasive and reflect free, biologically active cortisol. Hair cortisol testing offers a look at long-term cortisol accumulation over weeks or months. Fecal cortisol testing tracks patterns over time, useful in monitoring chronic stress. There is more work to be done to standardize the less invasive options, such as saliva testing or hair testing, for private practice.13,14

The Bigger Picture

Cortisol is not the enemy. It is the body’s brilliant way of matching internal resources to external demands. The problem is not that cortisol exists — it is that modern life for many pets keeps the system stuck in the on position, or that disease knocks the production up or down out of range.

The good news is that many of the levers that bring cortisol back into balance are within your reach. A calmer household. A more predictable routine. Positive training. Enrichment. A trusted veterinarian who checks the basics as your pet ages. Your presence, steady and reassuring, when the world gets loud.

If something has been changing about your dog or cat lately and you cannot quite figure out what, it is worth asking whether their internal chemistry may be part of the story. One hormone will not explain everything. But cortisol explains more than most people realize, and paying attention to it may unlock changes you have been trying to understand for a while.

  • 2,7,9,10 Animal Wellness Magazine, August 14, 2026
  • 3,5,6,11,12 Animals (Basel), 2024 Dec 7;14(23):3536
  • 13 Michigan State University, Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory, Testing for Hyperadrenocorticism ("Cushing's Disease") in Dogs
  • 14 Animals (Basel). 2025 Apr 23;15(9):1197

item.title: Is Your Favorite Animal Breaking Any of These Hilarious Laws?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Many of the animal-related laws on the books in the US were written long ago and have virtually no application in today’s world
  • Some of our earliest laws governing animal behavior and human behavior toward animals are truly head-scratchers
  • Several ordinances target specific animals and settings, such as banning flamingos from barbershops or restricting gorillas to the front seat of a car
  • A handful of laws set oddly literal rules, including a required parking fee for elephants tied to meters and mandatory taillights for roaming cats
  • Many statutes reflect long-standing local customs, from nighttime barking curfews to bans on frightening pigeons

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published October 17, 2015.

There are a lot of nutty laws on the books, but some of the most bizarre city ordinances and state statutes ever written concern animal behavior or human behavior toward animals.

Is That a Gorilla in Your Back Seat?

Pet360 offers up these doozies:1

  1. If you visit barbershops in Juneau, Alaska, don’t even think about bringing your flamingo with you.
  2. If you live in Arkansas and your cow likes to stroll down Main Street on Sunday mornings, just make sure he’s home before 1:00 pm. And in Little Rock, all dogs must stop barking after 6:00 pm.
  3. In Colorado, animal control officers must post a notice on a tree for 3 days prior to impounding a stray dog. Presumably that's to give dogs who can read a heads-up.
  4. There are probably no such signs in Hartford, Connecticut, however, because it’s against the law there to educate dogs.
  5. If you’re in Columbus, Georgia with an intact female cat, it’s your responsibility to insure neither she nor her male friends howl after 9:00 pm.
  6. If you’re fishing in Idaho, take care not to do it while sitting on a camel.
  7. If you attend the opera in Chicago, don’t expect to see any Poodles, as they’re not allowed. And Maryland residents who go to the movies must leave their pet lions at home.
  8. Under no circumstances should horses in Iowa be allowed to eat fire hydrants.
  9. Gorillas in Massachusetts may sit in the front seat only, never in the back seat of any car.
  10. Photographers in Wyoming are prohibited from snapping pictures of rabbits from January to April. Unless they have an official permit, of course.

Where Do They Sell Taillights For Kitties?

Online magazine Dogtime.com collected these jewels:2

  1. In California, it’s against the law for animals to make whoopee within 500 yards of a church or school.
  2. If you’re a feral or indoor/outdoor cat in Sterling, Colorado, you must put on your taillight before roaming the neighborhood.
  3. One town in Oklahoma prohibits gatherings of dogs in groups of 3 or more on private property unless they get a signed permit from the mayor. In another Oklahoma town, it’s illegal for humans to make “ugly faces” at dogs. (I kind of like that one!)
  4. Under no circumstances are cats allowed to chase dogs up telephone poles in International Falls, Minnesota.
  5. In the town of Barber, North Carolina, cats and dogs are prohibited from fighting each other.

Are There Whales in Nebraska?

TheDogPlace has an extensive list of “outrageous, crazy, and positively silly laws,” including:3

  1. If you live in Arizona, you should know that it’s illegal to hunt camels, and your donkey cannot sleep in the bathtub.
  2. In Hollywood (the one in California), it’s illegal to drive more than 2,000 sheep down Hollywood Boulevard at one time.
  3. If you ride your elephant to town in Florida and tie him to a parking meter while you run errands, be advised that the parking fee must be paid just as it would for a vehicle. If you live in Georgia, it’s against the law to tie your giraffe to a telephone pole or street lamp (no mention of a parking meter, however). If you reside in Louisiana, you may not tie your alligator to a fire hydrant.
  4. In Zion, Illinois, you are prohibited from offering your lighted cigar to your dog, cat, or other pet.
  5. In Massachusetts, it’s illegal to frighten a pigeon. (I like this one, too!)
  6. In Nebraska, it’s against the law to go whale fishing.
  7. If you live in Nevada, you should know that driving your camel on the highway is prohibited.
  8. In Marysville, Ohio, it’s illegal for dogs to urinate on parking meters. (Oddly, there are no parking meters in Marysville.) And in Paulding, a police officer may bite a dog to quiet him. (Good luck with that one!)
  9. In Pennsylvania, if you’re driving your vehicle and see a horse in the roadway, you must pull over to the side of the road and cover your vehicle with canvas. If the horse is still spooked by your car, you must start taking it apart piece-by-piece until he calms down.
  10. In Utah, birds have the right-of-way on all highways.

Sources and References

  • 1 Pet360,22 Craziest Animal Laws (Archived)
  • 2 Dogtime.com, March 25, 2014
  • 3 TheDogPlace, Ridiculous and Outrageous Animal Laws (Archived)

item.title: A Taste of the Tropics Gets a Paw Up!
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Mango is rich in beta-carotene (vitamin A precursor), a compound that also gives the fruit its bright color. Research has shown that it’s a major source of antioxidants that may promote wellness in animals
  • Another antioxidant in mango is quercetin, which has cognitive benefits as well as anti-inflammatory qualities
  • The main bioactive compounds found in mangoes are polyphenols, such as mangiferin, catechins, quercetin, kaempferol, gallic acid and benzoic acid, which are compounds associated with the prevention of degenerative diseases
  • When feeding mango to your pet, give them the flesh only. The large seed in the middle can be a choking hazard
  • While mango can be a tasty snack for your pet, be careful with the amount you're giving them because mango contains a fair amount of sugar, totaling 1.41 grams per tablespoon

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published May 19, 2022.

When it comes to tropical fruits, mango is certainly one of the more popular yet unique picks. Its deep yellow color and sweet, soft flesh are hallmarks of this fruit, which you can enjoy in various ways. Whether eaten raw, thrown in a blender to make a healthy smoothie or tossed in a salad, mango has something for everyone.

But does mango offer something for your pet as well? Based on the published research, the answer is yes. Small pieces of mango can be given as occasional healthy treats, or added to your pet's species-appropriate, nutritionally adequate meals in small amounts as food toppers. However, there are some things you need to know before adding this fruit to your pet's diet.

Did You Know?

The name mango most likely comes from the word "manna," which is the Malayalam word for the fruit. The Portuguese adopted this word as "manga" when they arrived in Kerala in 1498.1

Mangiferin Is Mango's Main Health-Promoting Compound

Bioactive compounds are the health-promoting molecules found in plants. Extensive research has been done regarding these compounds in an effort to learn what they can do for optimal health, both for humans and animals.2 In the case of mango, one of its main bioactive compounds is mangiferin.

According to a study published in 2017, mangiferin may play several roles and has antioxidant, antimicrobial, antidiabetic, anticancer and immunomodulatory properties.3 While there's no research done specifically on companion animals regarding mangiferin, lab tests were done on rats, which may give us some insight on how it may benefit dogs and cats.

For example, research published in the Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine noted that mangiferin has a cardioprotective effect in animal models, and the compound helped increase tissue antioxidant levels, as well as other markers such as lipid profile, histological score and mortality.4

In a 2003 study, again testing mangiferin, researchers discovered that it has anthelminthic and antiallergic properties. They administered mangiferin to test rats infected with Trichinella spiralis, a roundworm parasite, which led to a decrease of parasitic larvae in the musculature. In addition, oral treatment had an inhibiting effect on mast cell degranulation.5

Gallic Acid in Mango May Be Good for Pets

Another bioactive compound present in mango is gallic acid.6 Similar to mangiferin, it may provide health benefits to your pet, and one study done on animals showed promising results. In a 2022 paper published in Frontiers in Immunology, gallic acid (GA) was tested on dogs and was able to reduce oxidative stress and inflammatory response caused by environmental stressors.7

Another benefit that researchers noted is improved gut health. During the course of their study, they observed that the fecal matter of the puppies had a lower presence of pathogenic bacterial strains with a simultaneous uptick in probiotic strains.8

Mango Has Another Antioxidant — Quercetin

According to a 2017 study from Nutrients, one of the antioxidants inherent in mango is quercetin,9 which research has shown to have multiple health benefits among humans, such as anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties.10 What's interesting about quercetin is that it can benefit animal health as well.

In one animal model study, quercetin was shown to have a neuroprotective effect, which may have potential for treating Alzheimer's disease in humans, but may also benefit other species' cognitive health. To provide further context, researchers observed that quercetin inhibited amyloid-beta production, which resulted in better cognitive function in the test animals.11

In another paper, dogs that received a diet enriched with polyphenols (including quercetin), along with antioxidants and polyunsaturated fatty acids, managed atopic dermatitis better.12 Quercetin has also been observed to have anti-inflammatory potential, especially when combined with ascorbic acid (vitamin C).13

Mango Fun Fact

Mango first entered Western culture thanks to Portuguese explorers who brought the fruit from Asia to Brazil in the 16th century. From there, it was grown in Barbados in 1742, then spread to Mexico in the 19th century.14

How to Serve Mango to Your Pet

When buying mangoes at the grocery store or farmers market, you're safe with choosing regularly grown varieties. According to the Environmental Working Group, mangoes rank No. 12 in their "Clean Fifteen" list, which is a compilation of produce with the least amount of pesticides based on their testing methods.

"When giving mango to your pet, only the flesh should be eaten, ideally raw, so they can get the full benefits of the fruit."

To safely share mango with your pets, peel the fruit and remove the large seed (or pit) from the center of the fruit as it's a choking hazard.15 Make sure to chop the fruit into tiny, bite-sized pieces. Here's how you can dice a mango easily:16

  1. With the mango stem on top, cut vertically about a quarter of an inch away from the midline.
  2. Do the same slice on the other side.
  3. Using a knife, cut the flesh in a grid pattern without going through the skin.
  4. Use a large spoon to scoop out the mango cubes and place into a container.

While mango can be a tasty snack for your pet, be careful with the amount you're giving them. As a general rule, treats should be less than 10% of your pet's daily caloric intake. Another reason for following this rule is because mango contains a fair amount of sugar, totaling 1.41 grams per tablespoon.17

Top Mango Producers in the World

India is the world's top producer of mangoes, with a harvest of nearly 20 million tons annually. China is at second place, but their production is just above 4 million tons. Third place belongs to Thailand at around 3.5 million tons.18

The Sustainability of Growing Mangoes

Mangoes are readily available around the world, but have you ever wondered what their effects on the environment are? If you're conscious about your carbon footprint, when it comes to mangoes, don't worry. The industry surrounding this fruit has a minimal impact on the environment.

According to an environmental paper published by the National Mango Board, total gas emissions from mango production (from farms to retailers) average 0.45 kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of harvest. This is lower compared to tomatoes, which range between 0.8 to 5.6 kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of harvest, or beef, which is around 14 kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of product.19

Furthermore, planting more mango trees may benefit the environment. According to the same paper, the trees can help with carbon sequestering.20 Based on these findings, it's safe to say that the mangoes you're buying contribute to sustainability.

Your Pet Can Have Mango, but in Moderation

Mangoes are best enjoyed in raw form, which is also the best way to give this sweet fruit to your pet, in very small amounts, because of the sugar content. Dehydrated mango has a much higher sugar content and should be avoided for pets.

item.title: This Eye Injury Exposes Sensitive Nerves and Takes Months to Heal
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Corneal ulcers are a very common eye injury in dogs, and are typically caused by trauma to the eye, a foreign body, infection, dry eyes and abnormal structure of the eye
  • The seriousness of a corneal ulcer depends on how many layers of the cornea are involved
  • Symptoms of a corneal ulcer include squinting or pawing at the eye, watery eyes, sensitivity to light and a red, inflamed eye
  • Treatment depends on the underlying cause and the seriousness of the ulcer; ulcers that take a long time to heal can often be effectively treated with eye drops made from the patient’s own serum
  • Natural eye drops and other natural remedies plus an antioxidant-rich diet can also be very beneficial in both healing corneal ulcers and preventing their recurrence

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 17, 2018.

The cornea of your dog's eye is the outermost covering or layer, and all the other parts of the eye, including the iris and pupil, lay behind it. The cornea is actually transparent (see-through) and admits light into the eye. It also serves as a barrier to protect the structures inside the eye from bacteria, chemicals, foreign objects or any other agent that could cause damage and interfere with your dog's vision. The cornea is composed of four layers:

  1. Epithelium, which is the outermost layer
  2. Basement membrane, which lies directly below the epithelium
  3. Stroma, which comprises most of the thickness of the cornea
  4. Descemet's membrane, which is the innermost layer

How Corneal Ulcers Occur

Wounds to the cornea, which are typically caused by an abrasion, scratch, puncture or other trauma to the eye, are called corneal ulcers. Other causes for ulceration include:

  • Foreign body in the eye
